{{Short description|Characteristic of undirected graphs}}
{{Graph connectivity sidebar}}
In [[graph theory]], a branch of mathematics, the '''rank''' of an [[undirected graph]] has two unrelated definitions.  Let {{math|''n''}} equal the number of [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] of the graph.

* In the [[matrix theory]] of graphs the rank {{math|''r''}} of an undirected graph is defined as the [[Rank (linear algebra)|rank]] of its [[adjacency matrix]].  
:Analogously, the [[Nullity (graph theory)|nullity]] of the graph is the nullity of its adjacency matrix, which equals {{math|''n'' &minus; ''r''}}.

* In the [[matroid theory]] of graphs the rank of an undirected graph is defined as the number {{math|''n'' &minus; ''c''}}, where {{math|''c''}} is the number of [[Connected component (graph theory)|connected components]] of the graph. Equivalently, the rank of a graph is the [[rank (linear algebra)|rank]] of the oriented [[incidence matrix]] associated with the graph.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Grossman | first1 = Jerrold W.
 | last2 = Kulkarni | first2 = Devadatta M.
 | last3 = Schochetman | first3 = Irwin E.
 | doi = 10.1016/0024-3795(93)00173-W
 | journal = Linear Algebra and Its Applications
 | mr = 1324059
 | pages = 213–224
 | title = On the minors of an incidence matrix and its Smith normal form
 | volume = 218
 | year = 1995| doi-access = free
 }}. See in particular the discussion on p. 218.</ref>
:Analogously, the [[Nullity (graph theory)|nullity]] of the graph is the [[Kernel (matrix)|nullity]] of its oriented incidence matrix, given by the formula {{math|''m'' &minus; ''n'' + ''c''}}, where ''n'' and ''c'' are as above and ''m'' is the number of edges in the graph. The nullity is equal to the first [[Betti number]] of the graph. The sum of the rank and the nullity is the number of edges.

== Examples ==
A sample graph and matrix:
[[Image:Labeled undirected graph.svg|thumb|250px|An undirected graph.]]

(corresponding to the four edges, e1–e4):
{|
|
{| align=left class=wikitable
|-
! !! 1 !! 2 !! 3 !! 4
|-
!1
|0||1||1||1
|-
!2
|1||0||0||0 
|-
!3
|1||0||0||1 
|-
!4
|1||0||1||0
|}
| =
|
<math>
\begin{pmatrix}
 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\
 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\
 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\
\end{pmatrix}.
</math>
|}

In this example, the matrix theory rank of the matrix is 4, because its column vectors are linearly independent.
